newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Democracy activists protest China's HK legislature.
newsitem.headline: Democracy activists protest China's HK legislature.

text.p: Hong Kong pro-democracy demonstrators burned documents and shouted slogans on Monday in protest against a China-controlled committee meeting held to craft the colony's post-1997 political institutions.

About 20 banner-waving pro-democracy activists plunged the lobby of the China Building in Hong Kong's Central business district into chaos, scuffling with private security men, who called in police reinforcements as crowds of onlookers gathered.

The action came as the Preparatory Committee received final applications for seats on a provisional legislature that China plans to install when it takes back Hong Kong next July 1, ending more than 150 years of British rule.
China is to disband Hong Kong's legislature, elected under Governor Chris Patten's democratic reforms which Beijing says breached the Joint Declaration agreement on the handover.
"Phoney election", "dictatorship in disguise", demonstrators shouted, as they were barred from going upstairs to hand a petition to the committee's secretariat.
"Disband the Selection Committee", "universal suffrage for chief executive and post-97 legislature," they shouted.

Monday was the last day for seat seekers on the provisional legislature to apply. A 400-member Selection Committee will pick the 60 winners on December 21. The same body is meeting this Wednesday to select Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader.

The activists, from the United Front Against the Provisional Legislature, accused China of disenfranchising Hong Kong's 6.3 million people in favour of a "small circle election", and said people seeking seats on the new legislature were traitors.
"This is the narrowest election for the privileged and for business people," the petition said. It said the method would fuel Asia-style "money politics" or vote-buying in Hong Kong.
The China Building houses the head office of the Hong Kong blue chip conglomerate Cheung Kong Holdings, headed by tycoon Li Ka-shing, a kingmaker in the post-1997 leadership stakes.

The protesters ended their action peacefully and dispersed after burning large copies of an application form for the legislature seats with chants of "oppose the provisional legislature" and "oppose the reversal of democracy".

"After December 21, Hong Kong will be the only place in the world with two legislatures operating at the same time. It is a joke," protester Andrew Cheng, a legislator of the Democratic Party, told reporters.

He accused China of breaching the Joint Declaration, which it signed with Britain. "The Joint Declaration stipulates that the legislature shall be elected but the provisional legislature is not elected," he said.
"How can China have credibility? How can the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region have any credibility?" he asked.
